question: What are the NACEP standards and how were they developed?
expected_answer: NACEP standards are measurable criteria for quality concurrent enrollment partnerships. The first national standards were adopted in 2002 and revised in 2009 and 2017. The current standards have 16 standards in six categories, in effect since fall 2018. In 2019 NACEP added standards for the College Provided Faculty model.
source_doc: NACEP Standards for Quality; NACEP Accreditation FAQ; NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026
page_section: Standards page CEP and CPF sections; FAQ Q3; CEP Guide pp. ii to iii

question: What are the benefits of becoming a NACEP-accredited program?
expected_answer: Accreditation guarantees to students, policy-makers and other postsecondary institutions that the partnership meets rigorous national standards. It distinguishes the partnership, helping it recruit new partners and students. It helps students and families get their concurrent enrollment credits recognized. Accredited programs can display the NACEP logo, and their staff get national leadership opportunities such as serving on the Board or as a committee chair.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ; NACEP Accreditation Commission Overview
page_section: FAQ Q4; Commission Overview, Benefits of Accreditation

question: Are NACEP standards worth understanding and instituting even if a program is not interested in accreditation?
expected_answer: Yes. NACEP standards represent best practices for educational partnerships. The self-study process works both as a program evaluation against the standards and as a framework for program growth.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ

question: What is the difference between a concurrent enrollment program that is accredited and one that is not?
expected_answer: Accredited programs have completed a rigorous self-study and NACEP peer review and documented that their high school courses match the quality and rigor of the same courses on campus. Other programs may be just as good, but accreditation gives validation from an outside national organization. Some states require NACEP accreditation by law.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ

question: How are programs approved for accreditation? What is the process and what do reviewers look for?
expected_answer: A Peer Review Team of two to three experienced concurrent enrollment professionals, appointed by the Accreditation Commission and from outside the applying system, reviews the application. They decide whether the evidence meets the intent of each standard, may ask for more documentation, and keep asking questions during the site visit. They then send a final report to the Accreditation Commission, which votes on accreditation.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ; NACEP Application Process and Resources

question: How long does it take to apply for and receive NACEP accreditation?
expected_answer: Programs start preparing one to two years before applying. The accreditation cycle takes about 24 months. In year one the program submits a Letter of Intent (due December 1) and prepares and submits the application, which typically takes 4 to 6 months. In year two the peer review takes place, the Commission votes in April, and the decision is emailed in early May.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ; NACEP Application Process and Resources
page_section: FAQ Q8; Application Process, Accreditation Cycle and Steps 1, 3, 4, 7

question: How long do programs need to be in existence before applying for accreditation?
expected_answer: At least three consecutive school years.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources; NACEP Accreditation FAQ; NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026
page_section: Application Process, Eligibility & Fees; FAQ Q9; CEP Guide p. 6

question: How much does it cost?
expected_answer: Programs must first be NACEP members, at $560 a year. The Letter of Intent fee is $350. The application processing fee is $600 per endorsement for initial accreditation and $500 per endorsement for reaccreditation. Accredited programs pay a $500 annual accreditation fee plus membership, $1,060 a year in total. All fees are non-refundable and took effect September 1, 2026. Per nacep.org as of 2026-10-19. Check the site for current figures.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources; NACEP Accreditation FAQ
page_section: Application Process, Eligibility & Fees and Step 7; FAQ Q10

question: What happens if an application for accreditation isn't successful?
expected_answer: The program is notified and receives the review team's report with recommendations. If it believes the evidence was misinterpreted, it may request reconsideration by a new peer review team, as described in the Accreditation Reconsideration and Appeals Process in NACEP's Accreditation Policy and Procedures Manual. A denied or withdrawn applicant may apply again in the following year's review cycle.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation FAQ

question: What does CEP standard F2 require?
expected_answer: CEP F2 requires faculty liaisons to give all new concurrent enrollment instructors course-specific training in course philosophy, curriculum, pedagogy and assessment before they teach the course. Required evidence: sample training materials and an agenda for each discipline, the faculty liaison's description of how new instructors are trained, and an attendance report with the date each new instructor was trained.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026

question: What does CPF standard C2 require?
expected_answer: CPF C2 requires an academic administrator to review or conduct faculty evaluations and classroom observations following college policy. Required evidence: the published policy and procedures, and a sample of evaluations and observations with personal information redacted. The college sets the frequency, but the reviews must be done by an academic administrator, not CPF staff, and must be tracked.
source_doc: NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022

question: How do I file a complaint about an accredited program?
expected_answer: Use the complaint form on NACEP's Accreditation Commission page. Complaints must be about systematic concerns that an accredited program, or one under initial review, is not meeting NACEP standards. NACEP does not accept disputes between an individual and an institution, or anonymous complaints.
source_doc: NACEP Accreditation Commission Overview

question: What are the rules for the accreditation site visit?
expected_answer: The accreditation site visit is virtual and required for initial accreditation and reaccreditation. Visits run from January to mid-March, last one or two days, and cost nothing. The Lead Commissioner and the Peer Review Team attend, and the meetings are not recorded.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources

question: When is the Letter of Intent due and what does it cost?
expected_answer: The Letter of Intent for the 2027-2028 cycle is due December 1, 2026. It costs $350 and is non-refundable. It is submitted through your NACEP organization account starting September 1. Per nacep.org as of 2026-10-19. Check the site for current figures.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources

question: When do we find out if we got accredited?
expected_answer: The Accreditation Commission votes in April. The findings letter and decision are emailed in early May, and the national press release goes out in early June.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources

question: What do we have to pay and do each year once we're accredited?
expected_answer: Each year accredited programs pay a $500 accreditation fee plus the $560 membership fee, $1,060 in total. They must keep meeting the standards, submit an Annual Report each fall, volunteer every three years as a peer reviewer or Board, Commission or committee member, and tell NACEP at accreditation@nacep.org about substantial changes. Per nacep.org as of 2026-10-19. Check the site for current figures.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources

question: What's the difference between CEP and CPF?
expected_answer: In CEP, high school teachers teach college courses to high school students. CEP standards were first adopted in 2002 and revised in 2009 and 2017, and there are 16. In CPF, college faculty who are not employed by the high school teach college courses to high school students, in any location or delivery method. CPF standards were adopted in October 2019, and there are 13. Both use the same six categories.
source_doc: NACEP Standards for Quality; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: Standards page CEP and CPF sections; CPF Guide p. 1

question: How does standard F2 differ between CEP and CPF?
expected_answer: CEP F2: faculty liaisons give new instructors course-specific training before they teach. Evidence is training materials and agenda per discipline, a liaison description, and an attendance report. CPF F2: the program makes sure instructors know and follow college policies for teaching high school students (FERPA, Disability Services, Grading, Student Conduct). Evidence is new-instructor administrative orientation materials and a description of how instructors are informed.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: CEP Guide p. 13; CPF Guide p. 11

question: Does CPF have an annual professional development standard like CEP F3?
expected_answer: No. CPF faculty standards are F1 and F2 only. CEP F3 requires annual discipline-specific professional development for all instructors. If applying for both, one annual professional development event can include CEP and CPF instructors.
source_doc: NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022; NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026
page_section: CPF Guide pp. 1, 7; CEP Guide pp. 7, 14

question: How do classroom visits compare between CEP C3 and CPF C2?
expected_answer: CEP C3: faculty liaisons do site visits to check the course matches campus. The program sets the frequency for new and veteran instructors. Evidence: a typical visit description, how visits are tracked and how often, the latest visit date per instructor with the visitor's name and title, and one report per discipline. CPF C2: an academic administrator, not CPF staff, does evaluations and observations under college policy. The college sets the frequency and it must be tracked.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: CEP Guide p. 19; CPF Guide p. 13

question: What are the eligibility requirements for NACEP accreditation?
expected_answer: NACEP member in good standing with dues current through the cycle. Offered CEP or CPF for at least three consecutive academic years. All standards' policies in place before applying. Documentation the practices were in place the preceding academic year. Attended an Accreditation Institute within 24 months before the Letter of Intent. Institution accredited by a regional or institutional accreditor recognized by the US Department of Education and authorized by the state higher ed agency.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources; NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: Application Process, Eligibility & Fees; CEP Guide p. 6; CPF Guide p. 6

question: If we apply for both CEP and CPF, can we reuse documentation?
expected_answer: Yes for P1, P2, S1, S2, S4, E1 and E2 when a single process, procedure or policy is used. For S3 and S4, describe the differences between the models and why. One annual professional development event can cover CEP F3 and CPF F2.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: CEP Guide p. 7; CPF Guide pp. 1, 7

question: We have campuses with separate OPE IDs. Can we apply on one application?
expected_answer: Possibly. Separate OPE IDs are treated as separate institutions unless they show a clear, consistent, seamless connection (uniform curricula, unified professional development, uniform publications, shared assessment reported as one unit). A single application must show consistent policies. The Program Context describes variations and each cover sheet explains consistency for that standard.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
page_section: CEP Guide p. 7; CPF Guide p. 6

question: Can the high school principal pick who teaches our dual credit English class?
expected_answer: No. Academic departments or deans must approve CEP instructor appointments. Appointments based only on HR's or a high school principal's recommendation aren't acceptable.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026

question: Is giving new teachers the course syllabus enough training?
expected_answer: No. For CEP F2, providing or reviewing a syllabus alone isn't enough. The faculty liaison has to train new instructors on course philosophy, curriculum, pedagogy and assessment before they teach.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026

question: Our dual credit program started two years ago. Can we apply this year?
expected_answer: No. Programs need at least three consecutive academic years of operation.
source_doc: NACEP Application Process and Resources; NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026
page_section: Application Process, Eligibility & Fees; CEP Guide p. 6

question: Do professors have to visit every high school class every year?
expected_answer: No. The program defines site visit frequency for first-time and veteran instructors (CEP C3). Rotations like every 3 years are allowed if tracking covers all years. When visits aren't annual, new instructors should get a visit in their first year.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026

question: What does F2 require?
expected_answer: F2 differs by endorsement. For CEP, F2 requires faculty liaisons to give new instructors course-specific training in course philosophy, curriculum, pedagogy and assessment before they teach. For CPF, F2 requires the program to make sure instructors know and follow college policies for teaching high school students.
source_doc: NACEP CEP Accreditation Guide v7 rev 8-2026; NACEP CPF Accreditation Guide v2 Nov 2022
